title: Charles Darwin
summary: English naturalist who established that species change over time through natural selection, published in On the Origin of Species in 1859.

facts.label: Years between the idea and publication

age6_8.summary: A scientist who worked out how animals and plants slowly change over a very long time.
age6_8.body:
Charles Darwin loved studying animals and plants [1].

When he was young he sailed around the world on a ship called the Beagle. He collected beetles, birds, fossils and rocks [1].

He noticed something. Animals on different islands were a little bit different from each other.

Darwin worked out why. In every family, the babies are all slightly different. The ones that suit their home best are most likely to grow up and have babies of their own [2].

Do that for a very, very long time, and animals slowly change.

That idea is called evolution.

age9_12.summary: The naturalist whose theory of natural selection explained how species change.
age9_12.body:
Charles Darwin was an English naturalist who explained how living things change over time [1].

## The voyage

In 1831, aged 22, Darwin joined HMS Beagle as a naturalist on a surveying voyage. It lasted almost five years [1].

He collected specimens everywhere the ship stopped: fossils of huge extinct mammals in South America, birds and tortoises in the Galápagos Islands, coral reefs in the Pacific.

A common story says Darwin realised the theory while looking at Galápagos finches. That is not quite true. He did not even label which island each bird came from, and worked much of it out years later back in London [1].

## The idea

Darwin's argument has three simple steps:

1. Living things produce more offspring than can survive.
2. Offspring vary — no two are identical.
3. Some variations make survival and reproduction more likely.

If all three are true, then over many generations the helpful variations become more common. Darwin called this **natural selection** [2].

No one is choosing. It is simply what happens when some individuals leave more descendants than others.

## Twenty years of waiting

Darwin worked out the core idea by the late 1830s but did not publish for about two decades. He kept gathering evidence, and he knew the idea would be controversial [1].

In 1858 he received a letter from another naturalist, Alfred Russel Wallace, who had reached the same conclusion independently. Their work was presented together, and Darwin published *On the Origin of Species* the following year [2].

## What he did not know

Darwin had no idea how traits were inherited. Genetics was not understood until decades later. That his theory survived the discovery of genes — and was strengthened by it — is a large part of why it is trusted today [2].

teen.summary: English naturalist who established descent with modification by natural selection as the mechanism of evolutionary change.
teen.body:
Charles Darwin (1809-1882) was an English naturalist and geologist whose theory of evolution by natural selection provides the unifying explanatory framework of modern biology [1].

## The Beagle voyage

Darwin sailed aboard HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836. His role combined naturalist and gentleman companion to the captain [1].

His geological observations were as consequential as his biological ones. Reading Lyell's *Principles of Geology*, he became convinced that the Earth was extremely old and shaped by gradual processes still operating — a deep-time framework without which natural selection has no room to work [1].

The popular account of a Galápagos epiphany is largely retrospective construction. Darwin did not record which island most specimens came from; the ornithologist John Gould identified the finches as distinct species only after Darwin's return, and Darwin's thinking developed over subsequent years [1].

## Natural selection

The argument is deductive. Given that populations produce more offspring than survive; that heritable variation exists; and that some variants confer differential reproductive success — then the frequency of advantageous variants must increase across generations.

Darwin's insight was recognising that this suffices. No directing agency and no goal is required. Complex adaptation results from the accumulation of small advantages over long spans of time [2].

## Publication

Darwin developed the theory by 1838 but delayed publication for about twenty years, accumulating evidence and, on the available record, anticipating hostile reception [1].

In 1858 Alfred Russel Wallace sent Darwin an essay containing essentially the same mechanism, derived independently. Joint papers were read to the Linnean Society that year, and *On the Origin of Species* was published in November 1859 [2].

The episode is a clear case of independent co-discovery, and Wallace's contribution is frequently understated.

## The gap Darwin could not close

Darwin had no viable theory of inheritance. The blending inheritance assumed in his time would dilute any new variation within a few generations, a serious objection he never satisfactorily answered.

Mendel's work on particulate inheritance, published in 1866, went unnoticed until rediscovered around 1900. The reconciliation of Mendelian genetics with natural selection — the modern synthesis of the 1930s and 1940s — resolved the objection decisively [2].

That a nineteenth-century theory survived the discovery of an entirely unanticipated mechanism of inheritance, and was strengthened by it, is among the strongest arguments for its correctness.

adult.summary: English naturalist (1809-1882) who established descent with modification by natural selection, the central organising principle of the biological sciences.
adult.body:
Charles Robert Darwin was an English naturalist and geologist whose theory of evolution by natural selection constitutes the foundational explanatory framework of modern biology [1].

## Formation and the Beagle voyage

Darwin abandoned medical studies at Edinburgh and read for a divinity degree at Cambridge, where his substantive education was in natural history under Henslow and geology under Sedgwick. He joined HMS Beagle in 1831 for a surveying voyage lasting until 1836 [1].

His geological work was central. Lyell's uniformitarianism supplied both the deep timescale natural selection requires and a methodological model: explanation of large effects by the extended action of presently observable causes. Darwin's own theory of coral atoll formation, developed during the voyage, was an early and successful application [1].

The conventional narrative of a Galápagos revelation does not survive examination of the record. Specimen labelling was inconsistent, the finches' taxonomic significance was established by Gould after Darwin's return, and the transmutation notebooks show incremental development over subsequent years [1].

## The structure of the argument

Natural selection follows deductively from three empirical premises: that reproductive capacity exceeds what the environment can sustain; that heritable variation exists within populations; and that variation affects survival and reproduction. Differential reproduction of heritable variants follows necessarily.

The achievement lies in recognising the sufficiency of this mechanism. Adaptive complexity, previously taken to require design, is accounted for by cumulative selection acting on undirected variation over geological time [2].

*On the Origin of Species* also advanced common descent, arguing that the pattern of homology, embryological similarity, biogeographic distribution and the fossil record is explained by branching descent from shared ancestors.

## Delay, Wallace, and publication

Darwin's essential formulation dates to 1838-1842, yet he published only in 1859. The delay is generally attributed to a combination of evidential caution and awareness of the theory's social and religious implications, though the relative weight of these motives is a matter of historical interpretation rather than documented fact [1].

Alfred Russel Wallace, working in the Malay Archipelago, arrived independently at substantially the same mechanism and communicated it to Darwin in 1858. Joint papers were read to the Linnean Society, and the *Origin* appeared the following November. The case is a well-documented instance of independent co-discovery [2].

## The inheritance problem

Darwin lacked a theory of inheritance adequate to his own mechanism. Under the blending inheritance generally assumed at the time, novel variation is halved each generation and selection has insufficient material on which to act — an objection pressed by Fleeming Jenkin that Darwin could not answer. His provisional hypothesis of pangenesis was unsuccessful.

Mendel's demonstration of particulate inheritance (1866) remained unrecognised until approximately 1900. Early Mendelians initially regarded genetics as an alternative to selection rather than its complement; the modern synthesis of the 1930s and 1940s, through the population genetics of Fisher, Haldane and Wright, established their mathematical compatibility [2].

## Assessment

Darwin's theory made a substantive prediction about a mechanism he could not observe: that a particulate, faithfully transmitted basis for heredity must exist. The subsequent discovery of genes, and later of DNA, confirmed rather than displaced the framework. Theories that survive the discovery of their own missing mechanism are rare, and this is the principal reason evolutionary theory occupies the evidential standing it does [2].
